opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this was back when I was finishing undergrad. I'd been really into robotics, and the way I'd been taught to think about it was very much the classical approach: you decompose the problem. You have a perception module, a state estimation module, a planner, a controller, and you hand-engineer each piece and try to make the interfaces clean. And the implicit belief was that progress came from being clever about the structure, from putting the right inductive biases in.

Reading Gwern's scaling hypothesis essay flipped that for me. The core claim is that, as you scale up compute, data, and parameters, these fairly simple, general architectures just keep getting better in a smooth, predictable way, and capabilities emerge that nobody explicitly designed in. GPT-3 was the motivating example: nobody built a module for arithmetic or translation, it just fell out of predicting the next token at scale.

So the question I started asking was: why would robotics be any different? If the bitter lesson holds everywhere else, then all this careful hand-decomposition is probably the thing that eventually gets steamrolled. The real bottleneck in robotics isn't cleverness in the pipeline; it's that we don't have the internet-scale data and the compute that language had. That reframed the problem for me from "how do I design a better grasp planner" to "how do you get enough data and a general enough model that the robot learns this end to end."

And honestly, it also pushed me toward working on large models directly. If you believe the scaling story, then the highest-leverage place to be is wherever the scaling is actually happening, building the general model that robotics will eventually sit on top of, rather than trying to brute-force robotics in isolation. You can see that playing out now: a lot of the most exciting robotics work is basically taking pretrained vision-language models and fine-tuning them into policies. The general prior does a huge amount of the heavy lifting.

r001.rationale: He says scaling general models is the way forward for robotics, and describes adapting pretrained vision-language models into robot policies.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I came out of a mechanical engineering background, and I was doing robotics at the time, and the way I thought about it was very much the classical way. You build a world model by hand, you do system identification, you write controllers, you think really carefully about dynamics and contact. And you make progress, but it's this grinding, bespoke progress where every new task or new body is its own PhD.

Then I read Gwern's post, and the thing that hit me wasn't really the claim that bigger models get better. It was the framing that the bitter lesson generalizes, that what we'd been doing was essentially trying to hand-code priors that a sufficiently large model trained on enough diverse data would just learn, and learn better than we could specify. And the uncomfortable part was that he was basically right about language already. GPT-3 had come out, and you could see it doing things that nobody had explicitly built in.

So the update for robotics was something like: the bottleneck is not control theory, the bottleneck is data and scale. If you think of a robot policy as just another sequence model, then all the questions change. It's no longer "how do I design a better grasp planner," it's "how do I get the equivalent of the internet for physical interaction." Where does that data come from? Video? Simulation? Teleoperation? Fleets of cheap robots? And that's a very different research program than the one I'd been on.

The other thing it did was make me much more comfortable with being wrong in the direction of ambition. The post has this tone where it's almost scolding the field for not taking the straightforward extrapolation seriously because it felt too simple or too expensive. And I recognized myself in that. I'd been dismissing scale as a cop-out, like the real intellectual work was in the clever algorithm. And I came around to thinking the clever algorithm is often just a compression of what you'd learn anyway with more data, and it comes with a ceiling.

Honestly it's a big part of why I ended up moving toward working on the models themselves rather than on robots directly. If the hypothesis is right, the thing that unlocks robotics is the same thing that unlocks everything else, and you want to be as close to that as possible.

r001.rationale: The response says robotics progress depends on scaling models trained on diverse physical-interaction data, but it does not clearly identify those models as multimodal.

astra-6.text:
The big shift for me was from thinking, “What clever robotics-specific algorithm are we missing?” to thinking, “How do we build a system that keeps improving as we give it more data and compute?”

In robotics, it’s very tempting to build a lot of structure into the solution: here’s the perception system, here’s the planner, here’s the controller. You can make progress that way, but you’re also making a lot of decisions on behalf of the learning system. The scaling hypothesis suggested that maybe the central problem was finding a sufficiently general learning setup and then making it possible to scale.

That doesn’t mean you just say “scale” and robotics is solved. The hard question becomes where the experience comes from. With language, you have the internet. With robots, you have to collect interactions with the physical world, or figure out how to transfer learning from simulation and other sources. So it changed what I thought the bottleneck was: less about inventing the perfect controller, more about building the data and training loop that would let a general system learn to control things.

r001.rationale: The response describes scaling a general learning system with more data and compute to improve robotics, but it does not state that the approach is to scale large multimodal models.

sol-6.1.text:
It changed the question for me from “What clever algorithm are we missing?” to “What would let us apply enough scale to this problem?” In robotics, you can spend a lot of time building specialized machinery for individual tasks. The scaling perspective suggests that you should instead look for a general learning setup that keeps improving as you add data and compute.

That doesn’t make robotics easy. It shifts the bottleneck: how do you collect enough useful experience, across enough different situations, that the model can actually generalize? Then the robot, the data collection process, and the training system become parts of the same problem. You’re trying to build something where doing more of it reliably makes the system better.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes shifting toward a scalable general learning setup using more data and compute, but does not state that scaling large multimodal models is the way to solve robotics.
